core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Biliary Colic (Cholelithiasis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes analgesia, antiemetics, dietary fat restriction, and elective outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe right upper abdominal pain radiating to back and nausea after eating fried chicken

Key HPI features: 48F reports sudden, severe, squeezing pain in her right upper abdomen that radiates to her right shoulder blade. Pain started 1 hour after eating fried chicken and has lasted for 3 hours, accompanied by vomiting.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.1C, HR 88, BP 130/82. Abdominal exam reveals mild right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound, guarding, or a positive Murphy's sign. Labs: LFTs, amylase, and lipase within normal limits. RUQ ultrasound demonstrates gallstones without gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Biliary Colic (Cholelithiasis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute cholecystitis (persistent pain, fever) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever or pain lasting over 6 hours — suggests progression to cholecystitis.
management_principles: Order right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound (evaluate for gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, sonographic Murphy sign), check LFTs, amylase/lipase
Provide analgesia and antiemetics, advise a low-fat diet, and refer for elective outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Provide return precautions for fever, jaundice, or pain lasting beyond a few hours, which would suggest acute cholecystitis or choledocholithiasis
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Temporary obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone causing RUQ pain radiating to the back or shoulder after fatty meals, resolving once the stone dislodges.
red_flags: Fever or pain lasting over 6 hours — suggests progression to cholecystitis

must_ask.say: Did the pain start after eating fried or fatty food?
Does the pain spread to your back or shoulder?
How long has the pain lasted?
Has this happened before after fatty meals?

history.answer: I came in because I have intense pain in my upper right belly that started after eating fried chicken, and I feel nauseous.
It started suddenly about three hours ago, around an hour after I finished dinner.
The pain is right under my ribs on the right side, and it radiates through to my right shoulder blade.
It is a severe, deep squeezing pain that stays constant and does not come and go in waves.
I would rate it an eight out of ten, and it has stayed steadily severe the entire three hours.
Eating that greasy fried chicken definitely set it off, and lying still or changing positions has not helped at all.
I have had mild stomach tightness and indigestion after eating heavy meals before, but never pain this terrible or lasting this long.
I felt very nauseous and threw up my dinner once about an hour ago, with no blood or dark green fluid.
My bowel movement was normal this morning, I have had no diarrhea, and I am still passing gas.
No, I haven't had any fever or chills.
My eyes and skin haven't turned yellow, and my urine is its usual light yellow color.
I have no burning when I urinate, no need to go more frequently, and no blood in my urine.
No, I have not felt dizzy, lightheaded, or faint.
No, I haven't had any abnormal vaginal bleeding or unusual discharge.
I don't have any chest pressure, palpitations, or shortness of breath.
I ate greasy fried chicken for dinner about four hours ago, and I did not have any alcohol with it.
I haven't taken any pain relievers, aspirin, or anti-inflammatory drugs today.
No, I have never had an irregular heartbeat, atrial fibrillation, or any blood vessel problems.
I thought maybe I had severe indigestion from the grease, or perhaps an issue with my gallbladder.
I'm worried that a gallstone might be stuck and blocking something inside.
I was hoping to get an ultrasound scan to see what is going on and get some pain relief.
I don't have high blood pressure or diabetes, but my doctor has told me I am mildly overweight.
I have never had surgery or stayed overnight in a hospital.
I am not taking any daily prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I do not drink any alcohol.
I am a homemaker and I live with my husband and two teenage children.
My mother had gallstones and had her gallbladder removed in her fifties, and my father has high blood pressure.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, my periods are regular, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 130/82 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and body temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius.
Sclerae are white without icterus and conjunctivae are pink without pallor.
Abdomen is mildly obese and flat, with no surgical scars, visible distension, or pulsations.
Normal active bowel sounds heard throughout all four abdominal quadrants with no bruits.
Mild tenderness on deep palpation in the right upper quadrant without involuntary muscle guarding or abdominal rigidity.
No rebound tenderness is present in any quadrant of the abdomen.
Negative Murphy sign, with no arrest of inspiration upon deep palpation beneath the right costal margin during a deep breath.
No tenderness at McBurney point, and psoas and obturator signs are negative.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle fist percussion bilaterally.
Normal sphincter tone with an empty vault, no masses or tenderness, and no blood on the examining finger.
